topic: Decibels, power, RMS and PEP (G5B; 14 pool questions)

notes.front: What is a sine wave?
notes.back: A smooth, symmetrical waveform that rises to a positive peak and falls to a negative peak once each cycle — the standard shape of AC.
notes.explanation: The effective, peak and peak-to-peak formulas used for AC voltage and power all assume this shape.
notes.example: The AC from a household outlet is a 60 Hz sine wave (50 Hz in many other countries).
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 2 glossary: "The curve traced by the projection on a uniform time scale of the end of a rotating arm, or vector. Also known as a sinusoidal wave."

notes.front: What is the RMS value of an AC signal?
notes.back: The value that produces the same power dissipation (heating) in a resistor as a DC voltage of the same value.
notes.explanation: It lets AC and DC be compared directly for power purposes, since a plain average of a sine wave is zero.
notes.example: 120 V RMS mains delivers the same heating in a resistor as 120 V DC would, even though the AC swings well above and below 120 V.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G5B07; US Navy NEETS Module 2 glossary: "EFFECTIVE VALUE — Same as root-mean-square."

notes.front: What is the peak value of an AC waveform?
notes.back: Its maximum instantaneous value, reached once each half-cycle; for a sine wave it equals 1.414 times the RMS value.
notes.explanation: It is the highest instantaneous stress a component sees, even though the RMS value is what determines average heating.
notes.example: 120 V RMS mains reaches about 170 V at its peak.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 2 glossary: "PEAK VALUE — The maximum instantaneous value of a varying current, voltage, or power. It is equal to 1.414 times the effective value of a sine wave."

notes.front: What is the peak-to-peak value of an AC waveform?
notes.back: The full swing of the waveform, from its most positive point to its most negative point — twice the peak value.
notes.explanation: It is what most oscilloscopes read directly off the screen.
notes.example: A sine wave with a 170 V peak swings a total of 340 V peak-to-peak.

notes.front: What is average power?
notes.back: The power a signal delivers over time, found from its RMS voltage and current.
notes.explanation: For an unmodulated carrier, average power and PEP (peak envelope power) come out equal.
notes.example: A transmitter putting out a steady, unmodulated 100 W carrier has an average power of 100 W.

notes.front: How many dB corresponds to a doubling or halving of power?
notes.explanation: This is one of the few decibel values worth memorising directly, since it comes up constantly in link-budget and signal-report questions.

notes.front: What percentage power loss corresponds to a loss of 1 dB?
notes.explanation: A 1 dB feed-line loss figure, common on coax data sheets, means roughly a fifth of the power never reaches the antenna.

notes.front: How does the total current relate to the branch currents in a circuit of parallel resistors?
notes.back: Total current equals the sum of the currents through each branch.
notes.explanation: Each branch draws current independently, so the source must supply the total of what all the branches take.

notes.front: What three formulas find DC power from voltage, current and resistance?
notes.back: P = I × E; P = E² / R; P = I² × R.
notes.explanation: Pick whichever formula uses the two quantities you already know.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G5B03, G5B04, G5B05

notes.front: Why are AC voltage and current ratings normally given as RMS values?
notes.back: Because RMS is the value that gives the same heating effect as an equal DC value, so AC and DC power become directly comparable.
notes.explanation: A plain average of a sine wave is zero, so a different kind of average is needed for power calculations.

notes.front: For a sine wave, peak = {{c1::1.414 × RMS}}, and peak-to-peak = 2 × peak.
notes.explanation: These two ratios let you convert between any of the three ways of stating an AC voltage.

notes.front: How do you calculate PEP from the peak-to-peak voltage measured across a load?
notes.back: Halve the peak-to-peak voltage to get peak, multiply by 0.707 to get RMS, then apply P = E² / R.
notes.explanation: PEP uses the RMS value of the strongest part of the envelope, not the peak-to-peak figure directly.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G5B06, G5B12, G5B14

notes.front: How does PEP compare to average power for an unmodulated carrier?
notes.back: They are equal: the ratio of PEP to average power is 1.00.
notes.explanation: With no modulation, the envelope never rises above its steady level, so the peak and average powers coincide.

notes.front: What dB change represents a factor of two increase or decrease in power?
notes.choices:
A) Approximately 2 dB
B) Approximately 3 dB
C) Approximately 6 dB
D) Approximately 9 dB
notes.choicesExplained: A: 2 dB is too small a change for a doubling of power. C: 6 dB corresponds to roughly a factor of four, not two. D: 9 dB corresponds to roughly a factor of eight, not two.
notes.explanation: A power ratio of 2 works out to about 3 dB using the decibel power formula.

notes.front: How does the total current relate to the individual currents in a circuit of parallel resistors?
notes.back: It equals the sum of the currents through each branch
notes.choices:
A) It equals the average of the branch currents
B) It decreases as more parallel branches are added to the circuit
C) It equals the sum of the currents through each branch
D) It is the sum of the reciprocal of each individual voltage drop
notes.choicesExplained: A: total current is the sum of the branch currents, not their average. B: adding parallel branches increases total current, it does not decrease it. D: it is branch currents, not reciprocals of voltage drops, that add.
notes.explanation: Each parallel branch draws its own current from the source, so the source supplies their total.

notes.front: How many watts of electrical power are consumed if 400 VDC is supplied to an 800-ohm load?
notes.choices:
A) 0.5 watts
B) 200 watts
C) 400 watts
D) 3200 watts
notes.choicesExplained: A is the load's current (E / R) in amperes, not its power. C and D come from misapplying the power formula; only P = E² / R gives the correct 200 W.

notes.front: How many watts of electrical power are consumed by a 12 VDC light bulb that draws 0.2 amperes?
notes.choices:
A) 2.4 watts
B) 24 watts
C) 6 watts
D) 60 watts
notes.choicesExplained: B is ten times too large, a decimal-point slip on the correct answer. C and D do not follow from P = I × E with these values at all.

notes.front: How many watts are consumed when a current of 7.0 milliamperes flows through a 1,250-ohm resistance?
notes.choices:
A) Approximately 61 milliwatts
B) Approximately 61 watts
C) Approximately 11 milliwatts
D) Approximately 11 watts
notes.choicesExplained: B has the right digits but watts in place of milliwatts, a units slip of 1,000. C and D come from misapplying the power formula.
notes.explanation: P = I² × R = (0.007 A)² × 1,250 ohms ≈ 0.061 W, or about 61 mW.

notes.front: What is the PEP produced by 200 volts peak-to-peak across a 50-ohm dummy load?
notes.choices:
A) 1.4 watts
B) 100 watts
C) 353.5 watts
D) 400 watts
notes.choicesExplained: A comes from using the wrong voltage stage of the calculation. D (400 W) skips the halving step, treating the full 200 V p-p as if it were the peak voltage before the 0.707 conversion. C does not follow from any single slip.
notes.explanation: First halve the peak-to-peak reading, then apply the 0.707 conversion, then square and divide by resistance: 200 ÷ 2 = 100 peak; × 0.707 = 70.7 RMS; 70.7² ÷ 50 ≈ 100.

notes.front: What value of an AC signal produces the same power dissipation in a resistor as a DC voltage of the same value?
notes.choices:
A) The peak-to-peak value
B) The peak value
C) The RMS value
D) The reciprocal of the RMS value
notes.choicesExplained: A and B use the wrong points on the waveform; only the RMS value matches DC heating. D inverts the correct value, which has no such meaning here.
notes.explanation: RMS stands for root-mean-square, the specific average that matches a DC voltage's heating effect.

notes.front: What is the peak-to-peak voltage of a sine wave with an RMS voltage of 120 volts?
notes.choices:
A) 84.8 volts
B) 169.7 volts
C) 240.0 volts
D) 339.4 volts
notes.choicesExplained: A divides where it should multiply. B gives only the peak value, not peak-to-peak. C simply doubles the RMS value, skipping the 1.414 conversion.
notes.explanation: First multiply by 1.414 to reach the peak reading, then double that figure: 120 × 1.414 = 169.7; × 2 = 339.4.

notes.front: What is the RMS voltage of a sine wave with a value of 17 volts peak?
notes.choices:
A) 8.5 volts
B) 12 volts
C) 24 volts
D) 34 volts
notes.choicesExplained: A halves the peak value instead of multiplying by 0.707. C and D come from doubling steps that do not belong in a peak-to-RMS conversion.

notes.front: What percentage of power loss is equivalent to a loss of 1 dB?
notes.choices:
A) 10.9 percent
B) 12.2 percent
C) 20.6 percent
D) 25.9 percent
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D are all plausible-looking percentages, but only 20.6 percent follows from converting 1 dB to a power ratio.
notes.explanation: A 1 dB loss corresponds to a power ratio of about 0.794, meaning roughly 20.6 percent of the power is lost.

notes.front: What is the ratio of PEP to average power for an unmodulated carrier?
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are the RMS and peak conversion factors, not the PEP-to-average ratio. D would mean the peak is twice the average, which is not true for a steady unmodulated carrier.
notes.explanation: With no modulation, the envelope never rises above its steady level, so PEP and average power are equal.

notes.front: What is the RMS voltage across a 50-ohm dummy load dissipating 1200 watts?
notes.choices:
A) 173 volts
B) 245 volts
C) 346 volts
D) 692 volts
notes.choicesExplained: E = √(P × R) = √(1200 × 50) = √60,000 ≈ 245 V. C (346 V) and D (692 V) are that voltage's peak and peak-to-peak values; A (173 V) multiplies 245 by 0.707 again.
notes.explanation: Rearranging the P = E² / R power formula for voltage requires a square root, which is where this kind of question is often missed.

notes.front: What is the output PEP of an unmodulated carrier if the average power is 1060 watts?
notes.choices:
A) 530 watts
B) 1060 watts
C) 1500 watts
D) 2120 watts
notes.choicesExplained: A halves and D doubles the average power, neither of which applies to an unmodulated carrier. C does not follow from the 1.00 PEP-to-average ratio at all.
notes.explanation: For an unmodulated carrier, PEP equals average power, so both are 1060 W.

notes.front: What is the output PEP of 500 volts peak-to-peak across a 50-ohm load?
notes.choices:
A) 8.75 watts
B) 625 watts
C) 2500 watts
D) 5000 watts
notes.choicesExplained: D treats the 500 V peak-to-peak voltage as if it were RMS (500² / 50 = 5000 W). A and C do not come from any single slip in the calculation.
notes.explanation: First halve the peak-to-peak reading, then apply the 0.707 conversion, then square and divide by resistance: 500 ÷ 2 = 250 peak; × 0.707 = 176.8 RMS; 176.8² ÷ 50 ≈ 625.

notes.front: For a sine wave, how do RMS, peak and peak-to-peak values compare?
notes.back: RMS is the DC-equivalent value; peak is 1.414 × RMS; peak-to-peak is twice the peak (2.828 × RMS).
notes.explanation: Mixing these up is the most common way to get a PEP or voltage-conversion question wrong.

notes.front: How does finding PEP differ for an unmodulated carrier versus a modulated signal measured across a load?
notes.back: Unmodulated: PEP simply equals the average power. Modulated: PEP is calculated from the peak-to-peak voltage of the strongest part of the envelope.
notes.explanation: Using the unmodulated shortcut on a modulated signal, or vice versa, gives the wrong power figure.
